zoroastrian_spityura.name: saws his brother Yima in two with the dragon Azhi Dahaka
zoroastrian_spityura.notes: In the Zamyad Yasht (Yt. 19.46) Spityura, brother of the first king Yima, joins the three-headed dragon Azhi Dahaka and saws Yima asunder, an act of fratricidal treachery for which he is named among the agents of the Lie.

sources.reference: Avesta, Zamyad Yasht (Yasht 19.46)

zoroastrian_thrita.name: the first healer, who drove back sickness and death
zoroastrian_thrita.notes: Thrita of the Sama house was the first who beat back disease, death, fever, and the heat that comes from the body; for him Ahura Mazda brought down from heaven the thousands of healing plants growing about the white Haoma, the tree of immortality (Gaokerena).

sources.reference: Avesta, Vendidad, Fargard 20

zoroastrian_thrita.name: healing by the knife, by herbs, and by the holy word
zoroastrian_thrita.notes: In the Avestan scheme of medicine attributed to him, healing is worked three ways: with the cutting knife, with healing plants, and with the sacred spell (mathra); as an early presser of haoma his medical power is tied to the life-giving plant.

sources.reference: Avesta, Vendidad (Fargard 7.44; Fargard 20); Yasna 9.10 (Hom Yasht)

zoroastrian_zal.name: reared by the Simorgh and endowed with her wisdom
zoroastrian_zal.notes: Exposed at birth on Mount Alborz for his white hair, Zal was carried off and raised in her nest by the wonder-bird Simorgh, who nourished him and instilled in him wisdom and counsel before returning him to his father Sam.

sources.reference: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh, the tale of Zal and Sam

zoroastrian_zal.name: summons the Simorgh by burning one of her feathers
zoroastrian_zal.notes: On parting the Simorgh gave Zal feathers from her breast; when he or his line stood in mortal need he had only to cast a feather on the fire and she would come to aid him, most famously to deliver Rostam at his birth and to counsel the wounding of Esfandiyar.

sources.reference: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (the birth of Rostam; the combat with Esfandiyar)

zoroastrian_zal.name: renowned for sagacity and the riddle-wisdom of the mobads
zoroastrian_zal.notes: Zal is portrayed as a wise champion who wins Manuchehr's court by answering the riddles of the priests (mobads), and whose counsel guides the heroes of Sistan across generations.

sources.reference: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh, the wooing of Rudaba and the testing of Zal

zulu_umvelinqangi.name: descends to the Uhlanga swamp and brings forth the primal reeds
zulu_umvelinqangi.notes: In the cosmogony where he is distinguished from Unkulunkulu, the sky-father Umvelinqangi comes down to the great swamp Uhlanga and creates the reed-bed from which the first man Unkulunkulu breaks off, making him the prior, originating power of creation.

sources.reference: Zulu traditional religion (Callaway, The Religious System of the Amazulu, 1868-70, where uMvelinqangi appears as the first source); comparative ethnographic summaries

zoroastrian_spenta_armaiti.name: Spandarmad (Sepandarmazgan), the feast of Earth and Women
zoroastrian_spenta_armaiti.cadence: annual; the day Spandarmad (5th) of the month Spandarmad (12th, ~late February)
zoroastrian_spenta_armaiti.notes: On the name-day coincidence of her day and her month, the earth-guardian Spenta Armaiti (Spandarmad) was honoured with a festival of the earth, farmers, and women; al-Biruni records that husbands gave gifts to their wives and the day was a time for courtship, while the wild rue (esfand/spand) is her emblem.

sources.reference: al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations; Greater Bundahishn

zoroastrian_sraosha.name: Srosh invocation for the soul and against the demons of night
zoroastrian_sraosha.cadence: nightly devotion; and the rites of the first three nights after death
zoroastrian_sraosha.notes: Sraosha, lord of prayer, is invoked in the Sraosh Yasht and the daily liturgy to guard the worshipper through the hours of darkness when the demons range; he watches over the soul for the three days after death and conducts it toward the Chinvat bridge, so the Srosh rites are central to Zoroastrian funerary observance.

sources.reference: Avesta, Yasna 57 (Sraosha Yasht); Yasht 11 (Srosh Yasht Hadhokht)

zoroastrian_thraetaona.name: Invocation of the Fravashi of Thraetaona against fever and disease
zoroastrian_thraetaona.cadence: as needed, against sickness and the serpent's bite
zoroastrian_thraetaona.notes: The Frawardin Yasht calls on the Fravashi of the holy Thraetaona for resistance against the itch, the hot and the cold fever, and the serpent's venom; the dragon-slayer is thus invoked apotropaically as a healer and protector against disease.

sources.reference: Avesta, Frawardin Yasht (Yasht 13.131)

zuni_moonlightmother.name: Reckoning of the months and rites by the moon's phases
zuni_moonlightmother.cadence: monthly, by the lunar phases that set the ceremonial calendar
zuni_moonlightmother.notes: With the Sun Father and Earth Mother she is one of the three great Zuni powers; the Moonlight-Giving Mother gives light by night, and her waxing and waning are watched to count the months and fix the dates of the ceremonial round alongside the Pekwin's sun-watching.

sources.reference: Stevenson, The Zuni Indians (BAE 23rd Annual Report, 1904); Bunzel, Introduction to Zuni Ceremonialism (1932)

attributes.name: The upraised club (mace)
attributes.notes: His weapon is the strong mace held aloft, with which after sunset he smites Aeshma and the demons of wrath; he bears the epithet 'of the strong mace' (darshi.dru).

sources.reference: Avesta, Yasna 57 (Sraosha Yasht)

sacredAnimals.name: The cock / rooster (Parodarsh)
sacredAnimals.notes: The rooster is the bird of Sraosha, created to oppose the demons; calling the dawn it rouses the faithful to prayer and good works, and works with the dog as Sraosha's helper against the Lie. Its killing or ill-treatment is forbidden.

sources.reference: Avesta, Vendidad (Fargard 18, the bird Parodarsh); Greater Bundahishn

attributes.name: The ox-headed mace and the bound dragon
attributes.notes: He is figured as the smiter of the three-headed, three-jawed dragon Azhi Dahaka, wielding the bull-headed mace (gorz) and binding the monster; in later art his banner is the gilded Drafsh-e Kaviani.

sources.reference: Avesta, Aban Yasht (Yasht 5.33-34); Ferdowsi, Shahnameh

attributes.name: Solar radiance and the golden goad
attributes.notes: Yima the Radiant (Khshaeta) bears the kingly Glory (khvarenah) 'with the appearance of the sun', and is figured with the gold-inlaid dagger/goad of Ahura Mazda by which he widened the earth and ordered the Vara.

sources.reference: Avesta, Vendidad Fargard 2; Zamyad Yasht (Yasht 19.31-38)

attributes.name: Snow-white hair from birth
attributes.notes: Zal is unmistakable for the white hair and pale skin he bore from birth, the sign that caused his exposure and gave him his name; Persian painting depicts him as the white-haired champion, often shown in the Simorgh's mountain nest.

sources.reference: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh, the birth of Zal

sacredAnimals.name: The Simorgh
sacredAnimals.notes: The benevolent wonder-bird Simorgh, his foster-mother, is Zal's constant emblem and protector, returning whenever a feather is burned.

sources.reference: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh

sacredPlants.name: Wild rue (esfand / spand)
sacredPlants.notes: The wild rue, esfand or spand, shares her name and is treated as her plant-emblem, set on the Nowruz spread; she is also associated with medicinal herbs and the bountiful soil itself.

sources.reference: Greater Bundahishn (flowers of the Amesha Spentas); al-Biruni, Chronology

sacredPlants.name: White jasmine
sacredPlants.notes: In the Bundahishn's list assigning a flower to each of the Bounteous Immortals, the white jasmine is the flower of Vohu Manah (Bahman).

sources.reference: Greater Bundahishn (the flowers of the Amesha Spentas, ch. 16)

attributes.name: The primal reed-bed (uhlanga) of the great swamp
attributes.notes: As 'he who was in the very beginning', the sky-father is bound to the uhlanga, the primordial reed-marsh he descended to and out of which creation (and the first man Unkulunkulu) sprang; he is otherwise known by the natural signs of thunder and earthquake rather than by any image.

sources.reference: Zulu traditional religion (Callaway, The Religious System of the Amazulu, 1868-70); comparative ethnographic summaries

attributes.name: The moon itself
attributes.notes: She is the moon, the Moonlight-Giving Mother who lights the night; she has no idol but is known in her visible body and phases, counterpart to the Sun Father in the triad of the great Zuni powers.

sources.reference: Stevenson, The Zuni Indians (BAE 23rd Annual Report, 1904)
